allowed_dependency_manifest.content: Fix an integer n greater than 1. Let f_n(x) = floor(n times x) minus the sum for integer k from 1 to n of floor(k times x) divided by k. Consider f_n as a function on all real numbers x. Determine all real x values at which f_n(x) is globally maximal, and determine the corresponding maximal value M(n) = max over real x of f_n(x).

semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: For every integer n greater than 1, define f_n of a real input x as floor of n times x minus the sum over integers k from 1 to n of floor of k times x divided by k. Then for every real x and every integer z, f_n of x plus z equals f_n of x.
quantifier_order: for all integer n with n > 1

variables.name: z
variables.role: integer shift amount applied to x

variables.name: k
variables.role: summation index inside the definition of f_n

witness_dependencies: none (the claim is an equality for all choices of n, x, z; no existential witnesses are introduced)

payload.statement_nl: For every integer n>1, every real x, and every integer z, the function f_n defined by f_n(x) = floor(n*x) - sum_{k=1}^n floor(k*x)/k satisfies f_n(x+z) = f_n(x).

result_payload.proof_nl:
Fix an integer n>1, a real number x, and an integer z. We prove that f_n(x+z)=f_n(x).

Recall the standard floor identity: for every real t and every integer m, floor(t+m)=floor(t)+m. Indeed, if floor(t)=a, then a<=t<a+1, so a+m<=t+m<a+m+1, hence floor(t+m)=a+m.

Now for each k in {1,2,...,n}, since kz is an integer, we have
floor(k(x+z))=floor(kx+kz)=floor(kx)+kz.
Also, for k=n,
floor(n(x+z))=floor(nx+nz)=floor(nx)+nz.
Therefore
f_n(x+z)=floor(n(x+z)) - sum_{k=1}^n floor(k(x+z))/k
= floor(nx)+nz - sum_{k=1}^n (floor(kx)+kz)/k
= floor(nx)+nz - sum_{k=1}^n floor(kx)/k - sum_{k=1}^n z
= floor(nx)+nz - sum_{k=1}^n floor(kx)/k - nz
= floor(nx) - sum_{k=1}^n floor(kx)/k
= f_n(x).
So f_n is invariant under integer shifts: f_n(x+z)=f_n(x) for all real x and all integers z.
result_payload.proof_summary: Apply floor(t+m)=floor(t)+m with m=kz and m=nz termwise in the definition of f_n; the nz contributions cancel, giving f_n(x+z)=f_n(x).
